copy.headline: Man jailed for a year over punch that killed a Swede in Copenhagen

extended.text: Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday sentenced a 31-year-old man to a year in prison for a punch that killed Christian Zedig, a 32-year-old Swede. The man had pleaded guilty, and he is also barred from nightlife for a year.

On 30 June, at a big-screen showing of a World Cup match at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen, he threw two beer cans at a group that included Zedig. Then he punched him on the head or neck. The blow ruptured an artery. Zedig, who worked for the Swedish police, died on 3 July.

He was convicted of simple rather than aggravated violence. A punch is typically not dangerous, Søren Harbo, a special prosecutor with Copenhagen Police, told the court. The judge counted the man's aggressive behaviour and his earlier convictions, for attempted murder, rape and violence, against him.
Nicolai Wammen, the justice minister, says the government will raise the penalty when simple violence kills. In some such cases, he says, the sentence is 'unacceptably low'.

copy.headline: Police charge two Kosovar guards trained for Denmark's prison in Kosovo with beating an inmate

standard.text: Copenhagen Police have charged two prison officers from Kosovo with punching an inmate repeatedly in a cell at Vestre Fængsel, a Copenhagen prison, on Monday. Both deny it. A judge released them on Wednesday, finding no risk that they would flee.
They had trained in Denmark to guard inmates at a prison the government is renting in Gjilan, Kosovo, for foreigners sentenced to deportation. It is now expected to open in late 2027 or early 2028.

Ina Eliasen, director of the prison service, says it will look at whether its training of the officers is good enough. Anders Vistisen of Dansk Folkeparti, a nationalist party that backed the 2021 agreement, called Kosovo 'a complete misfire' as a destination.

short.text: Two prison officers from Kosovo have been charged with punching an inmate at Vestre Fængsel, a Copenhagen prison, on Monday. Both deny it. They had trained in Denmark to guard inmates at a prison the government is renting in Kosovo.

copy.headline: WHO says it cannot fully assess a suspected plague death in Russia

standard.text: The World Health Organization cannot fully assess the risk from a suspected plague death in Russia. 'We do not yet have the full picture,' Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, its head, said on Wednesday.

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia's Irkutsk region, died last week. Russia says she died of pneumonia of unknown cause; unnamed sources told local media she may have caught plague from a broken test tube.

The WHO and America want answers about a second laboratory worker reported to have pneumonia. Dmitry Peskov, the Russian president's spokesman, said Russia informed the WHO as procedures require and accused the media of spreading false information.

short.text: The World Health Organization says it cannot fully assess the risk from the suspected plague death of a 28-year-old technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia. Russia says she died of pneumonia of unknown cause.

copy.headline: Parliament drops anonymity for politicians in Afghanistan study

standard.text: The Presidium of the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, decided unanimously on Wednesday that former members of its confidential Foreign Policy Committee cannot be quoted anonymously in a study of Denmark's military mission in Afghanistan.

In May the Presidium had made naming them depend on their consent, arguing that they had spoken expecting 30 years of confidentiality. Veterans objected, 50,000 people signed a citizens' proposal against it, and in September the four governing parties pushed to reverse it.

Peter Kragelund, director of the Danish Institute for International Studies, whose researchers are writing the study, hopes to send it to print before Christmas, with publication probably in the new year.

short.text: The Presidium of the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, decided on Wednesday that former members of its confidential Foreign Policy Committee cannot be quoted anonymously in a study of Denmark's military mission in Afghanistan, reversing a decision from May. The researchers hope to send it to print before Christmas.

copy.deck: Former members of a confidential committee lose the option to be quoted anonymously; the researchers hope to send the study to print before Christmas.

copy.headline: Far-left party demands a ban on profit from welfare in budget talks

standard.text: Enhedslisten, a far-left party, will demand a ban on profit from publicly funded welfare in the coming budget negotiations. Private providers of supported housing, shelters, crisis centres and elderly care would have to run as self-governing institutions that reinvest any surplus.
Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, would not promise a ban but told Information she is 'not super keen' that money can be made 'from other people's misery'.

SF, a left-wing party, wants first to see whether a new rate model solves the problems. Radikale Venstre, a social-liberal party, accepts profit at crisis centres if it brings more places and better care.

short.text: Enhedslisten, a far-left party, will demand a ban on profit from publicly funded welfare, including crisis centres and elderly care, in the coming budget negotiations. Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, would not promise it.

copy.headline_short: Far-left party demands welfare profit ban
copy.deck: The party calls it one of its priority demands; the prime minister promises nothing.
